speech: Here's what I found. After months of waking up, scratching my skin.
Oh, your skin gets itchy at night? Maybe you even wake up with scratch marks you don't remember making.
I guess that's just sensitive skin, right? That's exactly what I kept telling myself.
Dry skin? I moisturized before bed, bought creams, made sure my skin wasn't dry when I went to sleep,
and still I'd get into bed and I'd start scratching again. Then I blamed the detergent,
so I switched it, changed the sheets, washed everything, put on fresh pajamas, same thing.
But during the day, my skin would calm down, then I'd get back into bed and it would start
all over again. Some nights it was my arms, other nights my legs.
Sometimes I'd get this weird, buzzing, irritated feeling across my face and chest.
Around four or five in the morning, I'd wake up already scratching before I was even properly awake.
Some nights, I'd scratch until it burned, put more cream on, turn over, try to fall asleep again,
then wake up scratching again. By morning, I'd feel like I hadn't slept at all. I dragged myself
through the day, exhausted, then dread getting into bed that night because I already knew what was
coming. But I still thought it was something with my skin. Until one night, I just couldn't take it
anymore. I got into bed, the itching started, and I laid there thinking I cannot do this again tonight.
So I got up, grabbed a yoga mat, rolled it out on the living room floor, grabbed a pillow,
and slept there on the floor. And that night, the itching stopped. That was the first time I thought.
Wait, this isn't just my skin. Maybe it's something about the bed. So next morning,
I stripped everything off, checked the sheets, checked the mattress, checked the pillows, saw
nothing. Everything looked completely normal. So I went online and searched, why does my skin
only itch when I'm in bed? I got the usual explanations, dry skin, detergent, fabric,
eat. But I'd already done all of those. So that left me with two possibilities. Either I was dealing
with some kind of allergy, or it was a skin condition, like dermatitis or eczema, that somehow only flared
up in bed. At that point, I was done guessing. So I called my doctor and suggested I get tested.
So I did. And when the results came back, dust mites. Dust mites? I thought those made people sneeze.
But then she explained that dust mites aren't just dust, they're alive and commonly found in mattresses,
pillows and bedding. A colony contains anywhere from 100,000 to 10 million dust mites. They live
deep in the fibers, feeding on the skin you shed every night. And because they're microscopic,
your bed can look perfectly clean and you'd never know they were there. The allergens irritate
and inflame skin for people sensitive to them. And suddenly, the last few months made sense.
Why I couldn't find anything. Why my skin would calm down during the day, then start acting up
again after spending hours back in bed. My doctor gave me the usual plan for reducing
dust mite exposure. Wash covers, keep the humidity down, vacuum, take antihistamines when I needed
them. So I did. But the itching didn't completely stop. I still woke up scratching. I just wanted to
understand what else I could do. So I read about them. The more I read, the more interesting it got.
Because I suddenly realized how difficult they are to deal with. A lot of the advice focused on
managing symptoms and reducing exposure. Not actually removing the mites,
already living in the mattress and fabric. The antihistamine calmed my reaction. Hot washes and
vacuuming cleaned the surface. Air purifiers removed the particles from the air. But none of those
things reached what was already inside the mattress and fabric. The colony I was reacting to
every night. That's why the itching came back the next night and why I never felt like I was
getting ahead of it. So eventually I started considering the other option. Replace the mattress.
And for a minute, I almost did. Then I remembered what I paid for that mattress. $2,000. And even
if I spent another thousand or two, what would stop the same thing from happening to the next mattress?
I wasn't ready to do that. Not without trying something else first. What I needed was something
that could reach the mites in the bed I already had. Something designed to pull them out instead
of simply cleaning around them. And that's when I came across something I'd never seen before.
They're called capture cards. Inside each card is a plant derived lure designed to attract
dust mites. The mites move toward the lure and once they reach the card, the adhesive traps them
inside. Then when you remove the card, the trapped mites come out with it. You lift the mattress,
slide the cards underneath near the corners and leave them there. That's it. No spraying your
skin. No spraying the mattress. Plus they came with a 90 day money that guarantee. So I thought,
you know what? Worth a shot. I ordered them. When they arrived, there really wasn't much to it.
I lifted the mattress, slid the cards underneath near the corners and left them there. No sprays,
no complicated cleaning routine, no taking the mattress apart. Then when it was time,
I swapped in a new one and threw the full one away. Finally, I wasn't just waking up itchy
troll over my bedroom, my nighttime routine, and the next morning. More than 30,000 homes
have already tried capture cards. And right now you can get them for up to 65% off. They also
come with a 90 day money back guarantee. You don't even have to return them. So if you're tired of
